Section 8(2)(g) does not apply to:
- personal information about any individual, if it would be unreasonable to publish the information (s 8(2)(g)(i)) (as a general rule this does not prevent publication of the names of Australian Government agency staff in connection with their official duties[13] although agencies may consult relevant staff where potential harm could arise from publishing their names)
- information about the business, commercial, financial or professional affairs of any person, if it would be unreasonable to publish the information (s 8(2)(g)(ii))
- other information that the Information Commissioner has determined it would be unreasonable to publish under s 8(3) (s 8(g)(iii)) (see [13.102]–[13.105] below).

[^13]: Explanatory Memorandum to the Freedom of Information Amendment (Reform) Bill 2009, p 7.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Information routinely given through FOI access requests
title: Information routinely given through FOI access requests
text: These exceptions indicate that agencies are generally not expected to publish information given to an individual or business in response to an FOI request that is personal to that individual or business.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Information routinely given through FOI access requests
title: Information routinely given through FOI access requests
text:
In deciding what information is ‘routinely’ accessed, agencies should have regard to the similar requirement in s 11C to publish a disclosure log of information released in response to FOI requests (see Part 14 of these Guidelines). The purpose of the IPS is also relevant to deciding what is routine. It forms part of an approach to information disclosure that recognises information held by Government is a national resource, and that agencies should proactively publish information that may be of public interest. The IPS is also designed to lessen the number of individual requests for documents made to agencies. Agencies should therefore take an expansive rather than a narrow view of what information is ‘routinely’ accessed. In particular, agencies should consider whether publishing the information would:
- promote the objects of the FOI Act
- be in the public interest
- reduce the likelihood of further requests for the information.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Information routinely given through FOI access requests
title: Information routinely given through FOI access requests
text: While the disclosure log will contain information an agency has released in response to individual requests, an IPS entry is to contain information that is ‘routinely’ released. That is, agencies are required to include in their IPS entry information that has been requested on multiple occasions. The information that was released may not have been identical on each occasion; it may have been revised or updated between requests, or the information may reflect a later development on the same topic. The kind of information that is routinely released in response to FOI requests will vary between agencies but may include statistical information about an agency’s service delivery performance that is regularly requested by the media or other members of the public (for example, the number of applications received and finalised, the percentage of applications granted, timeliness data, etc). Other examples may include minutes of meetings that are regularly requested under the FOI Act, Senate Estimates Briefs and consultation submissions (where these are not otherwise published).

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Information routinely given through FOI access requests
title: Information routinely given through FOI access requests
text: It is recommended as best practice that agencies review the FOI requests the agency receives to identify trends and topics of interest (for example, on a 6-monthly basis) and make this information publicly available through their IPS. Agencies may choose to use artificial intelligence tools to assist in identifying these trends and topics of interest to the public. Successful identification of routinely requested information has the potential to reduce the number of FOI requests made to the agency and result in more targeted FOI requests.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Information routinely given through FOI access requests
title: Information routinely given through FOI access requests
text: Review of FOI requests will also assist agencies identify commonly requested categories of personal information and to consider how the agency can use digital means, for example, self-service portals, to increase the accessibility and availability of this information to members of the public. In these cases, access to information can be provided without the need for an FOI request to be made under the FOI Act.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Information routinely given through FOI access requests
title: Information routinely given through FOI access requests
text: Publication of information on a disclosure log will sometimes satisfy the requirement in s 8(2)(g) to publish that information under the IPS. To avoid dual publication, an agency’s IPS entry may contain a link to the disclosure log and a reference to the information to which the agency has routinely given access. In some circumstances it may be better practice, in complying with s 8(2)(g), for the IPS entry to contain either an extract from the disclosure log or a separate summary of information that is routinely released by the agency in response to FOI requests.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Information routinely given through FOI access requests
title: Information routinely given through FOI access requests
text: Whichever approach is adopted, agencies must ensure that the information is accurate, up-to-date and complete (s 8B). Consequently, if information in the disclosure log has been revised or replaced, an IPS entry which links to the disclosure log will also need to be amended.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Information routinely given through FOI access requests > Exceptions — personal and business information
title: Exceptions — personal and business information
text: As with the disclosure log requirements, an agency is not required to publish personal or business information as part of its IPS entry if it would be unreasonable to publish that information (ss 8(2)(g)(i) and (ii)). As noted above at [13.92], agencies will generally not publish information given to an individual or business in response to an FOI request that is personal to that applicant.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Information routinely given through FOI access requests > Exceptions — personal and business information
title: Exceptions — personal and business information
text: The third-party consultation requirements that apply before a decision can be made under Part III of the FOI Act to release business documents or documents affecting personal privacy in response to an FOI request (ss 27 and 27A) do not apply to IPS and disclosure log publication decisions. It is nevertheless open to an agency to develop procedures to ensure that it has considered the views or interests of an FOI applicant or third party before publishing information under the IPS or disclosure log.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Information routinely given through FOI access requests > Exceptions — personal and business information
title: Exceptions — personal and business information
text: Where information is not published because an exception applies, agencies may record this in an IPS information register, including the title of the document to which an exception applies and the reason it was not published under the IPS (see [13.40]–[13.46]) above on information registers). Capturing this information may help an agency if it needs to respond to any complaints to the Information Commissioner about its IPS compliance.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Information routinely given through FOI access requests > Exceptions — Information Commissioner determinations
title: Exceptions — Information Commissioner determinations
text: The Information Commissioner may make a determination that the requirement to publish routinely accessed information under s 8(2)(g) does not apply to information specified in the determination (s 8(2)(g)(iii)). A determination of this kind is a legislative instrument for the purposes of the Legislation Act 2003 (s 8(3)). A determination may apply to information of a general kind that is held by many agencies, or to a specific kind of information held by a particular agency. A similar exemption applies to the requirement to publish information in a disclosure log (s 11C(2)) (see Part 14 of these Guidelines).

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Information routinely given through FOI access requests > Exceptions — Information Commissioner determinations
title: Exceptions — Information Commissioner determinations
text:
In deciding whether to make a determination, the Information Commissioner will have regard to:
- the extent to which publication of the information in question would further the objects of the FOI Act
- whether there is an established and reasonable public demand for the information
- the estimated resource requirement for an agency to publish the information and whether this would impose an unreasonable burden on the agency.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Information routinely given through FOI access requests > Exceptions — Information Commissioner determinations
title: Exceptions — Information Commissioner determinations
text: For further information about determinations under s 8(3), see the Information publication scheme and disclosure log determinations policy and procedure (available at Information Publication Scheme (IPS) and Disclosure Log determinations policy and procedure | OAIC).

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Information routinely given through FOI access requests > Exceptions — Information Commissioner determinations
title: Exceptions — Information Commissioner determinations
text: The Information Commissioner has not yet made a determination under s 8(3) of the FOI Act.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Parliamentary information
title: Parliamentary information
text:
Agencies are required to publish information they hold that is routinely provided to the Parliament in response to requests and orders from the Parliament (s 8(2)(h)). This includes, but is not limited to:
- Senate Order No 12: Production of departmental file lists
- Senate Order No 15: Appointments and vacancies
- Senate Order No 16: Approved grants
- Senate Order No 13: List of departmental contracts ($100,000 or more)
- Senate Order No 14: List of advertising/public information projects ($100,000 or more)[14]
- Information of a kind that is routinely requested from an agency by Parliament through a parliamentary committee.

[^14]: Parliament of Australia - Senate Orders for documents.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Parliamentary information
title: Parliamentary information
text:
Section 8(2)(h) does not apply to an answer provided to a Question on Notice in the Parliament, unless the question is of a recurring nature for information of a similar kind (including a question requesting an update or revision of information earlier provided in response to a question). Nor does s 8(2)(h) apply to an agency submission to a parliamentary committee. It is nevertheless open to an agency to publish that information in the IPS under s 8(4) of the FOI Act (other information). Agencies should also note that s 8(2)(h) operates alongside another guidelines that requires online publication of information presented to the Parliament — see Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, Tabling Guidelines.[15]

[^15]: See https://www.pmc.gov.au/publications/tabling-guidelines.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Parliamentary information
title: Parliamentary information
text:
In applying s 8(2)(h), agencies should adopt a similar approach to that for s 8(2)(g) (documents to which access is routinely given). In particular, an agency should consider including in its IPS entry information that was provided to the Parliament, if:
- this would promote the objects of the FOI Act
- the information is of public interest
- further requests or orders from the Parliament for the information are likely.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Parliamentary information
title: Parliamentary information
text: Agencies should establish internal procedures for ensuring that information routinely provided to the Parliament is identified as such and published under the IPS.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Parliamentary information
title: Parliamentary information
text:
If an agency is aware that information provided to Parliament has been published elsewhere (for example, on the Parliament’s website[16]), it may be appropriate to provide a link to that website.

[^16]: Agencies are advised to check what information is accessible and where it can be located on the Parliament’s website before providing links (for example, the majority of submissions to committees are published on the committee inquiry webpage).

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Contact officers
title: Contact officers
text: Agencies must publish contact details of an officer (or officers) who can be contacted about access to the agency’s information or documents under the FOI Act (s 8(2)(i)).

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Contact officers
title: Contact officers
text:
To meet this requirement, agencies should publish the name (or position title), telephone number and email address of the FOI contact officer or officers. Agencies should establish generic telephone numbers and email addresses (for example, foi@agency.gov.au) that will not change with staff movement. [17]

[^17]: See the model FOI page included in the Information Commissioner’s Guide to the access of information page on an agency's website | OAIC.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Contact officers
title: Contact officers
text: Where it is not appropriate to include the name and contact details for each FOI contact officer (for example, due to regular staff changes) the agency should provide contact details for the position.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information
title: Operational information
text:
An agency’s operational information must be published as part of an agency’s IPS entry (s 8(2)(j)). ‘Operational information’ is defined in s 8A(1) as:
… information held by the agency to assist the agency to perform or exercise the agency’s functions or powers in making decisions or recommendations affecting members of the public (or any particular person or entity, or class of persons or entities).

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information
title: Operational information
text: The publication of operational information ensures that members of the public are adequately informed about the rules, policies, principles and procedures that agencies apply in making decisions or recommendations that them.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information
title: Operational information
text: Publication of that information is important in its own right, but is also necessary to ensure that members of the public are not disadvantaged by a lack of awareness of the information used by agencies to make decisions or recommendations. Section 10 of the FOI Act reinforces that objective by providing that a person must not be subjected to any prejudice that could have been avoided had they been aware of operational information that should have been, but was not, published. What operational information an agency should publish, and the degree of specificity of that information, should therefore be viewed through the lens of whether a member of the public would be prejudiced by not having access to the information. Further information about s 10 of the FOI Act, see [13.139]–[13.140].

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information
title: Operational information
text: Operational information is all the information an agency holds, whether generated by the agency or not, that assists it to perform or exercise its functions or powers in making decisions or recommendations affecting members of the public (or any particular person or entity, or class of persons or entities). The ‘person’ affected by an agency decision may be an individual, an organisation or a business entity. Examples of operational information include rules, guidelines, practices and precedents relating to decisions and recommendations affecting members of the public (s 8A).

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information
title: Operational information
text:
Four terms in the definition of ‘operational information’ in s 8A(1) reflect the breadth of the concept:
- information held by an agency to ‘assist’ it ([13.119]–[13.121])
- in performing or exercising its ‘functions or powers’ ([13.122]–[13.124])
- in making ‘decisions or recommendations’ ([13.125]–[13.126])
- ‘affecting members of the public (or any particular person or entity, or class of persons or entities’ ([13.127]).

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > Information held by the agency to assist it
title: Information held by the agency to assist it
text: Information held by the agency to assist it make decisions or recommendations is deliberately broad. It is not confined to rules or precedents that can be applied directly to reach a decision but may also include other documents that facilitate good decision-making such as policy guidance, procedures, decision templates, model letters, training packages and checklists. If an agency has multiple versions of the same document with minor variations, publication is only required of a single contemporary or representative document.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > Information held by the agency to assist it
title: Information held by the agency to assist it
text: How agencies come to decisions that affect members of the public is critical to facilitate public understanding and trust in government. Without background knowledge of how decisions are being made, results can only be taken at face value and cannot be fully interrogated for fairness and accuracy and, ultimately, the results are not contestable. Section 10 of the FOI Act recognises this by providing that individuals must not be subjected to any prejudice if they lack awareness of unpublished operational information. Further information about s 10 FOI Act is at [13.139]–[13.140] below.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > Information held by the agency to assist it
title: Information held by the agency to assist it
text:
Operational information should therefore be interpreted to include information about the use of artificial intelligence tools (AI), generative AI and automated decision-making (ADM) systems that support decision-making and/or recommendations, including the rules and procedures that agencies apply in making decisions.[18] Further information is at [13.128]–[13.133] below.

[^18]: See ‘Automated decision-making and public reporting under the Freedom of Information Act’, Office of the Australian Information Commissioner, 21 January 2026, Automated decision-making and public reporting under the Freedom of Information Act | OAIC.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > Functions or powers of an agency
title: Functions or powers of an agency
text: An agency’s functions and powers must be published in the IPS under s 8(2)(c). As described above at [13.65]–[13.68], functions or power may be assigned to an agency by legislation, an executive instrument or in some other manner.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > Functions or powers of an agency
title: Functions or powers of an agency
text: There may be overlap in the documents that are required to be published under s 8(2)(c) and s 8(2)(j). Nevertheless, s 8(2)(c) provides a reliable starting point in identifying operational information that is required to be published under s 8(2)(j).

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > Functions or powers of an agency
title: Functions or powers of an agency
text: Formal instruments authorising officers within an agency to make decisions or take certain actions that affect members of the public fall within the definition of ‘operational information’ in s 8A(1) of the FOI Act and so should be included on an agency’s IPS entry. Bearing in mind the definition of operational information in s 8A, this requires publication only of those instruments in current use (not archived versions) and does not extend to instruments that do not affect members of the public. See also [13.135]–[13.138] below for further examples of information that does not fall within the definition of operational information in s 8A.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > Making decisions or recommendations
title: Making decisions or recommendations
text: The term ‘decision’ is to be understood broadly. For example, the Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977 s 4(2) defines ‘making a decision’ to include making, suspending, revoking or refusing to make an order, award or determination; giving, suspending, revoking or refusing to give a certificate, direction, approval, consent or permission; issuing, suspending, revoking or refusing to issue a licence, authority or other instrument; imposing a condition or restriction; making a declaration, demand or requirement; retaining, or refusing to deliver up, an article; and doing or refusing to do any other act or thing.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > Making decisions or recommendations
title: Making decisions or recommendations
text: The term ‘recommendation’ in s 8A(1) should be construed in a similarly broad manner.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > Affecting members of the public or a class of people
title: Affecting members of the public or a class of people
text: These are words of limitation. They confine the concept of operational information to decision-making that affects members of the public in an individual manner or as members of a particular group or class (including an organisation or business entity). Examples are decisions or recommendations that concern a right, privilege or benefit of a member of the public or a class of people, or an obligation or penalty to which a person or class of people may be subject.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > Affecting members of the public or a class of people > Automated decision-making systems and artificial intelligence
title: Automated decision-making systems and artificial intelligence
text:
Automated decision-making (ADM) is ‘the use of technology, commonly referred to in Commonwealth legislation as a ‘computer program’, to automate a decision-making process’.[19] Examples of ADM used by the Australian Government includes, but is not limited to, computer programs to calculate fees, AI systems to assess grant applications, and benefit or tax calculators.

[^19]: See Reform of automated decision-making legislation – Consultation paper, p 7.From 10 December 2026, the Privacy Act 1988 will require ADM use to be disclosed in agency privacy policies if:The entity has arranged for a computer program to make, or do a thing that is substantially and directly related to making, a decision andThe decision could reasonably be expected to significantly affect the rights or interests of an individual andPersonal information about the individual is used in the operation of the computer program to make the decision or do the thing that is substantially and directly related to making the decision.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > Affecting members of the public or a class of people > Automated decision-making systems and artificial intelligence
title: Automated decision-making systems and artificial intelligence
text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a broad umbrella term for machines designed to simulate human thinking. Generative AI is a subset of AI focused on generating content – such as text, images, software code, audio or video – based on patterns learned from large volumes of data.[20]

[^20]: See Staff guidance on public generative AI | digital.gov.au.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > Affecting members of the public or a class of people > Automated decision-making systems and artificial intelligence
title: Automated decision-making systems and artificial intelligence
text:
Agencies may use generative AI to support the performance or exercise of their powers or functions. Because generative AI use may be operational information,[21] the ways in which this technology is used to support the agency should be published on its IPS. The IPS reflects the objects of the FOI Act as it provides a statutory scheme that promotes transparency and accountability. In the context of ADM or AI, the IPS obligations should be interpreted as promoting the transparent use of these technologies that affect members of the public by Australian Government agencies or via Commonwealth contracts. For agencies that have already published an AI Transparency Statement that contains this information, their IPS can also link to that statement.[22]

[^21]: To the extent that generative AI is used to assist the agency perform or exercise its functions or powers to make decisions or recommendations that affect members of the public.
[^22]: The Digital Transformation Agency (DTA) has issued a policy for the responsible use of AI in government and has published information to support implementation of the policy - Standard for AI transparency statements | digital.gov.au.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > Affecting members of the public or a class of people > Automated decision-making systems and artificial intelligence
title: Automated decision-making systems and artificial intelligence
text: Examples of generative AI use by the Australian Government that would not be ‘operational information’ include the use of an AI product to generate emails promoting the agency’s services (that is, it does not relate to the making of decisions or recommendations) or AI being used to organise or categorise the agency’s information holdings (if that does not affect members of the public). Therefore the service or function being performed in part or in whole by AI or ADM is the commencement point for determining publication obligations. That approach furthers a purposive interpretation (with reference to the objects of the FOI Act) in determining whether the service or function affects members of the public. Additionally, the use of AI by a contracted service provider to deliver services or functions will generally be the agency’s operational information where there are contractual arrangements between the agency and the provider that give the agency rights to receive a document in accordance with the requirements of s 6C(2).

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > Affecting members of the public or a class of people > Automated decision-making systems and artificial intelligence
title: Automated decision-making systems and artificial intelligence
text:
In January 2026, the OAIC published a report on ‘Automated decision-making and public reporting under the Freedom of Information Act’ (the ADM report).[23] This report assesses how transparent Australian Government agencies are about their use of ADM in decision-making processes. In the report, the Information Commissioner made recommendations to help agencies publish policies and procedures as part of their IPS, to foster transparency and open government. These recommendations are:
- To ensure members of the public are not prejudiced by a lack of awareness of the use of ADM by agencies, all agencies authorised under legislative statutes to use ADM should publish this information as part of the IPS. This should include the name of the legislation that grants them this power, and whether or not they use ADM to provide information and services to the public.[24]Note: s 8A(2) of the FOI Act provides that an agency’s operational information does not include information that is available to members of the public otherwise than by being published by (or on behalf of) the agency. While legislation authorising agencies to use ADM to make decisions may be published elsewhere (for example, on legislation.gov.au), ADM use may not be apparent to an ordinary member of the public, who would have to read an entire Act to identify whether a decision an agency has made using ADM is authorised under relevant legislation. Agencies should therefore publish information about the legislation that authorises them to use ADM to make decisions that affect members of the public, broadly state the kinds of decisions they use ADM for, and publish any relevant guidelines, policies or rules about how ADM is applied to affect members of the public.If an agency is authorised to use ADM under legislation but does not in fact use ADM, the FOI Act does not require this to be published on the agency’s IPS. However, it is open to the agency to do so where it considers this may assist members of the public understand how it makes decisions.
- Agencies should clearly state the types of ADM they use to make automated decisions, not just that AI is being used by the agency.[25]The degree of specificity required will be determined by the type of decisions or recommendations being made and whether members of the public would be prejudiced if they were not aware ADM is being used. In this context, it may involve advice that a rules-based or machine learning system is used to make certain (specified) decisions. In some circumstances this may require the ADM system to be named. However this will usually not require publication of the rules and algorithms the ADM system relies on. Publishing technical details or algorithms may not assist members of the public understand how decisions are being made and may raise intellectual property, national security or fraud concerns.Section 8C(1) of the FOI Act provides that an agency is not required to publish exempt matter on its IPS. Therefore, if publication of information about how AI is being used, or details of the AI product, would breach a confidentiality agreement (s 45), disclose trade secrets (s 47(1)(a)) or would, or could reasonably be expected to, destroy or diminish the commercial value of information (s 47(1)(b)), it does not have to be published. In some limited circumstances, publishing this information would have a substantial adverse effect on the financial or property interests of an agency (s 47D) or disclose information that would, or could reasonably be expected to, have a substantial adverse effect on agency operations (s 47E(d). Where it is decided not to publish certain information, this should be added to the agency’s internal IPS information register (see [13.43]).
- Agencies that use ADM should publish both a list of decisions they use ADM for, as well as relevant and easy to understand examples where possible, so the public can better understand how ADM is being used to make decisions that affect them.[26]Where it is not possible to publish a list of all decisions made using ADM, the list can be a high level explanation of the types of decisions the agency makes using ADM, for example, decisions to grant or refuse a particular benefit under an Act or decisions to grant, revoke or vary a licence under an Act (which needs to be specified). To the extent that these decisions are ones that the Australian Privacy Principles (APPs) require entities to include in their privacy policy, compliance may be achieved by linking to the relevant information in the agency’s privacy policy. Likewise, where other legislation requires information about ADM use to be published, compliance with IPS obligations can be achieved by linking to that information.
- As part of their IPS, agencies using ADM should publish any policies that clearly set out the principles for when and how they use ADM to make decisions and recommendations affecting members of the public.[27] To the extent that this information is already published in the agency’s AI Transparency Statement, or is required by other legislation, including a link to that statement will satisfy this requirement.

[^23]: Automated decision-making and public reporting under the Freedom of Information Act.
[^24]: Recommendation 1 of the OAIC report Automated decision-making and public reporting under the Freedom of Information Act.
[^25]: Recommendation 2 of the OAIC report Automated decision-making and public reporting under the Freedom of Information Act.
[^26]: Recommendation 3 of the OAIC report Automated decision-making and public reporting under the Freedom of Information Act.
[^27]: Recommendation 4 of the OAIC report Automated decision-making and public reporting under the Freedom of Information Act.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > Affecting members of the public or a class of people > Automated decision-making systems and artificial intelligence
title: Automated decision-making systems and artificial intelligence
text: Agencies should specify the practical ‘operational’ use of ADM. Without this specific operational information, it is not possible to understand the details around an agency’s use of ADM. This specificity aligns with the FOI Act’s requirement for transparency about the rules, policies, principles and procedures that agencies apply in making decisions.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > Affecting members of the public or a class of people > Automated decision-making systems and artificial intelligence
title: Automated decision-making systems and artificial intelligence
text: Information held by a contracted service provider that assists it to provide services to the public on the agency’s behalf may be operational information which an agency must publish in its IPS entry. This will apply if the agency holds a copy of the information (whether generated by the agency or the contracted service provider) or is entitled to a copy under s 6C and the information otherwise falls within the definition of operational information in s 8A(1). If the agency does not have a copy of the information held by the contracted service provider, the agency may nevertheless arrange for that information to be published under s 8(4) (other information). This will advance the IPS objective of ensuring the public has easy and direct access to information that is used by or on behalf of Australian Government agencies to make decisions about rights, privileges, benefits, obligations and penalties that affect members of the public.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > What is not operational information?
title: What is not operational information?
text:
The concept of operational information does not encompass all government decision-making that directly or indirectly affects the public. The following categories of information are examples that would not ordinarily fall within the definition of operational information, even though the information may influence government decision-making:
- policy analysis and decisions occurring within government about legislation, budgets and programs
- discussions within government about the operation of a program or legislation
- case studies and capability reports that discuss an agency’s response to an actual or foreshadowed event
- audit and evaluation reports on the operation of a government program or compliance with legislative requirements
- agency case management procedures for recording the handling of an individual matter or the making of a decision.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > What is not operational information?
title: What is not operational information?
text: Documents that are not operational information can nevertheless be published by an agency under s 8(4) (other information).

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > What is not operational information?
title: What is not operational information?
text: The reference in the definition of operational information in s 8A(1) to information that assists an agency to make decisions or recommendations ‘affecting members of the public’ means that the definition does not extend to agency manuals and rules relating to personnel management and staff conditions of employment. Those manuals and rules relate to employees in their employment capacity and not as members of the public. Nor, for the same reason, does the definition extend to information held by the Merit Protection Commissioner relating to the review of decisions about APS employees. However, as noted at [13.143]–[13.152] such information can nevertheless be published by an agency under s 8(4) (other information).

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > What is not operational information?
title: What is not operational information?
text: Section 8A(2) provides that ‘[a]n agency’s operational information does not include information that is available to members of the public otherwise than by being published by (or on behalf of) the agency’. This exclusion applies to information such as law reports, books, guides and standards that are published by another body and that are used by agency officers in making decisions that affect members of the public.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > Failure to publish operational information
title: Failure to publish operational information
text: Section 10 provides that a person must not be subjected to any prejudice stemming from an agency’s performance of a function or exercise of a power that the person could have avoided if they had access to unpublished operational information. This rule applies, for example, where the eligibility requirements for a benefit or allowance (such as a closing date) are specified only in an agency publication which should have been, but were not, published under the IPS. The rule applies only if the person could lawfully have avoided the prejudice if they had been aware of the unpublished information.

heading: Information required to be published under the IPS > Operational information > Failure to publish operational information
title: Failure to publish operational information
text: The rule does not apply to the agency’s performance of a function or the exercise of a power unless the agency has existed for more than 12 months (s 10(1)(c)(ii)). The agency is nevertheless expected to publish operational information under the IPS as soon as reasonably practicable after it creates that information.

heading: Exceptions to publication under the IPS
title: Exceptions to publication under the IPS
text:
Section 8C(1) provides that an agency is not required to publish exempt matter in their IPS entry. Exempt matter is defined as, matter the inclusion of which in a document causes a document to be an exempt document (s 4(1)). An exempt document is:
- a document of an agency that is exempt under a provision in Part IV of the FOI Act. If a document contains both exempt and non-exempt matter the agency should prepare an edited copy (see Part 5 and Part 6 of these Guidelines) or
- an official document of a minister that contains information not relating to the affairs of an agency or a department of state (see Part 2 of these Guidelines) or
- a document in respect of which an agency, person or body is exempt under s 7 of the Act, such as an intelligence agency document or a document relating to the commercial activities of a specified body (see Part 2 of these Guidelines).

heading: Exceptions to publication under the IPS
title: Exceptions to publication under the IPS
text: Section 8C(2) provides that an agency is not required to publish information that is restricted or prohibited from publication by an enactment. That is, an agency is not required to publish information contrary to a legislative secrecy provision.

heading: Other information to be published under the IPS
title: Other information to be published under the IPS
text: The FOI Act does not limit or restrict what information an agency publishes, including information that is exempt from disclosure under the FOI Act (s 3A).

heading: Other information to be published under the IPS
title: Other information to be published under the IPS
text: Section 8(4) of the FOI Act authorises agencies to publish ‘other’ information. The power to publish other information under s 8(4) is in addition to any other power an agency has to publish information.

heading: Other information to be published under the IPS
title: Other information to be published under the IPS
text: Agencies and staff are protected against civil and criminal liability if they publish documents in good faith, believing publication is either required or permitted under the IPS (ss 90 and 92), see [13.192]–[13.194] below. However, if a document is subject to a secrecy provision, the protections in the FOI Act may not apply.

heading: Other information to be published under the IPS
title: Other information to be published under the IPS
text:
Agencies are generally best placed to identify other information that should be published under s 8(4). In doing so, agencies should strive to implement the objects of the FOI Act, which declare that information held by government is a national resource that should be managed for public purposes, and that the Parliament intends to increase scrutiny, discussion, comment and review of the Government’s activities (s 3). Agencies should also consider:
- open by design principles by prioritising, promoting and resourcing proactive disclosure of information held that is of value to the public[28]
- the Information Commissioner’s Principles on open public sector information, which encourage agencies to ensure government information is accessible without charge, based on open standards, easily discoverable, understandable, machine-readable, and freely reusable and transformable[29]
- the OAIC’s Information policy agency resource, Open data quick wins — getting the most out of agency publications, which explains how agencies can transform data they already publish in reports, websites and mobile apps into machine-readable formats that support reuse by others[30]
- advice about technical and other relevant matters that should be taken into account when publishing government information online.[31]

[^28]: See for example: ICIC endorses OAIC resolution on proactive publication | OAIC and Statement of principles to support proactive disclosure of government-held information | OAIC .
[^29]: Principles on open public sector information | OAIC.
[^30]: Open data quick wins – getting the most out of agency publications | OAIC.
[^31]: Available at Digital Service Standard | digital.gov.au.

heading: Other information to be published under the IPS
title: Other information to be published under the IPS
text:
The term ‘other information’ can include a wide range of information, which will vary from agency to agency. The following are examples of information required to be published in other Australian jurisdictions that Australian Government agencies should consider making available:
- A record of open access information that is not made publicly available because there is an overriding public interest against disclosure – Australian Capital Territory and New South Wales
- Register of cabinet decisions – Victoria
- A statement listing all boards, councils, committees, panels and other bodies that have been established by the agency (whether under an Act or otherwise) for the purpose of advising the agency or a Minister responsible for the agency – Australian Capital Territory
- Statement of advice, recommendations or reports held by an agency – Australian Capital Territory and Victoria
- Budget papers and Appropriation Acts – Australian Capital Territory
- Information about government grants made or administered by the agency – Australian Capital Territory
- Ministerial briefs – Australian Capital Territory
- Information an agency undertakes to make publicly available – Australian Capital Territory.

heading: Other information to be published under the IPS
title: Other information to be published under the IPS
text:
Examples of other information that agencies may consider adding to their IPS include Senate Estimates briefs and, for relevant regulators, the Ministerial Statement of Expectations and the responding Statement of Intent.[32]

[^32]: Further background is available at: Guidance Note | Department of Finance.

heading: Other information to be published under the IPS
title: Other information to be published under the IPS
text: As recommended earlier in these Guidelines (see [13.34] above), agencies should explain in their agency plan the steps the agency will take to review their information holdings and identify information that may be suitable for publication. This information should be described in the agency plan. To the greatest extent possible, information that is suitable for publication should be identified as such from early in its lifecycle and published as soon as reasonably practicable. The agency plan should also provide a timetable of when information will be published or updated.

heading: Other information to be published under the IPS
title: Other information to be published under the IPS
text:
Agencies should review whether they hold any datasets that can be published for reuse.[33] Publication of datasets on data.gov.au should be considered. [34] The agency website can link to that website to avoid duplication in publication. Agencies should ensure that published information is described according to the appropriate metadata standards to enable users to find it easily.

[^33]: See Australian Government Public Data Policy Statement which requires Australian Government entities to make non-sensitive data open by default. The Policy Statement is available at: Australian Government Public Data Policy Statement.
[^34]: For guidance about preparing open data and publishing datasets on data.gov.au see User guide | Data.gov.au.

heading: Other information to be published under the IPS
title: Other information to be published under the IPS
text:
Agencies should have regard to the following in deciding what information to publish:
- What information is of interest to members of the public and external stakeholders?
- Is there a public demand for categories of information held by the agency?
- Will publication of particular information assist the public in dealing with the agency or in commenting on programs or policies for which the agency is responsible?
- Will publication of particular information promote greater agency accountability, or better public understanding of agency decisions?
- Is information considered for publication in an appropriate format to make it accessible and reusable by the public?
- Will published information require revision or updating, or is it part of the historical record of agency activity?
- Are there privacy or security concerns that require information to be de-identified or aggregated before it is published?[35]

[^35]: For guidance about de-identifying data before publication, see De-identification and the Privacy Act | OAIC.

heading: Other information to be published under the IPS
title: Other information to be published under the IPS
text:
Publication of information under s 8(4) should not be a burdensome task for agencies. Agencies may consider releasing data in ‘beta’ form,[36] with appropriate caveats on its limitations. Engagement with stakeholders prior to publication may help agencies identify the data and formats for which there is the greatest demand.

[^36]: Beta testing provides an opportunity for users to use a product in a production environment to identify issues before general release. Beta testing is the final round of testing before releasing a product to a wide audience.

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry
title: Managing an agency IPS entry
text: This section discusses the principles agencies should observe in managing their IPS entry. Some of the principles are expressly required by the FOI Act, while some others are implicit in the objects of the FOI Act (s 3) and in Part II establishing the IPS.

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Performance of agency functions
title: Performance of agency functions
text: Section 10A provides that a function or power given to an agency under Part II of the FOI Act can be performed or exercised by the principal officer of the agency or by an agency officer in accordance with arrangements approved by the principal officer. This is an equivalent provision to s 23, which provides that a decision on a request to an agency for access to a document can only be made on behalf of the agency by an authorised person.

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Performance of agency functions
title: Performance of agency functions
text:
Unless the principal officer of an agency intends to exercise all functions and powers under Part II of the Act, they must approve arrangements under s 10A nominating the authorised persons in the agency and the scope of their authority. The functions and powers to be exercised under Part II include:
- preparation of an agency plan under s 8(1)
- publication of information required to be published by the agency under s 8(2), including deciding whether information is exempt from publication under s 8(2)(g)
- publication of other information by the agency under s 8(4)
- ensuring that information published by the agency is accurate, up-to-date and complete as required by s 8B
- ensuring that information published by the agency is published on a website in accordance with ss 8D(2) and (3)
- deciding whether the agency will impose a charge for providing access to information published by the agency (s 8D(4)), and publishing details of any charges the agency may impose (s 8D(5))
- arranging for regular review (at least once every 5 years) of the agency’s IPS (s 9)
- if the need arises, taking appropriate action under s 10 to ensure that a person is not subjected to any prejudice as a result of not having access to operational information that was not published as required by s 8(2)(j).

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Governance arrangements
title: Governance arrangements
text: Leadership at a senior level is critical in establishing a culture within an agency for full compliance with the IPS requirements in Part II of the FOI Act. Agencies should consider appointing an Information Champion, or establishing an information access governance board, to provide the leadership, oversight and accountability necessary to promote and operationalise proactive publication.

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Governance arrangements
title: Governance arrangements
text:
Staff in the Senior Executive Service (SES) are well placed to fulfill the important role that an Information Champion has in leading their agency to develop a culture that gives full effect to the pro-disclosure objects of the FOI Act, and the IPS in particular.[37]

[^37]: For agencies without SES level staff, the most appropriate senior staff member may be appointed as the Information Champion.

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Governance arrangements
title: Governance arrangements
text:
The OAIC has prepared specific guidance for SES staff to assist in setting the standard for IPS compliance within their agency and to shape their agency’s culture in relation to openness, transparency and accountability.[38]

[^38]: See Information Publication Scheme overview for senior executive staff | OAIC.

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Governance arrangements
title: Governance arrangements
text: Information Champions are responsible for ensuring the agency has appropriate governance mechanisms in place to ensure compliance with IPS obligations.

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Governance arrangements
title: Governance arrangements
text:
Information Champions can improve IPS practices by:
- informing staff of their responsibilities under the IPS
- publishing a broad range of documents on the agency’s website at the time of their creation
- establishing governance regarding the publication of new and revised operational documents
- ensuring there is a process for regular review of documents not considered suitable for publication on the agency’s IPS at a particular time, to consider whether those reasons continue to apply
- making the IPS a priority when developing corporate plans
- analysing the FOI requests received by the agency to assist in identifying information of interest to members of the public, and proactively publishing those documents
- ensuring that an agency’s IPS entry is accurate, up-to-date and complete
- considering compliance with the IPS as a performance indicator for agency employees.

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Publication on a website
title: Publication on a website
text:
Information published under the IPS must be published on a website (s 8D(3)). The information may be published on the agency website, on another website to which a link is provided, or by some other accessible means that are described on the website.[39]

[^39]: For guidance on accessible publication on the agency disclosure log see Part 14 (Disclosure Log) of the FOI Guidelines.

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Publication on a website
title: Publication on a website
text:
Many agencies maintain their own website and will publish their IPS entry on that website. As stated in the guiding principles to these Guidelines (see [13.15] above), the IPS entry should be easily discoverable by the public, consistent with the object of the FOI Act to facilitate and promote public access to information, promptly and at the lowest reasonable cost (s 3(4)). Adopting the following practices will assist in facilitating public access:
- Agencies should consider using the ‘Access to information’ icon published by the Information Commissioner to link to their IPS entry. It is recommended that the access to information icon be displayed on the agency’s homepage (in the footer). The Information Commissioner’s intention in publishing the icon is to aid the discoverability of agency IPS entries by encouraging a consistent approach across government.[40]
- An agency’s IPS entry can contain links to other pages on the agency website or other websites where the required information is available. This may be particularly useful in cases where an agency has already published information falling under the IPS requirements.
- The sitemap for the agency website should list information that the agency is required to publish under s 8(2) or has decided to publish under s 8(4).
- The search function on the agency website should facilitate access to information published in the agency’s IPS entry through key terms and descriptive metadata. To aid that search function, online content should be published in a format that can be searched. Further, agencies should consider optimising their websites so they can be accurately mined by search engines and AI tools.
- The agency should provide an alert service, such as an email notification service or RSS feed, to notify subscribers of new publications under the IPS or other developments in relation to the agency’s compliance with the IPS. If the alert service provided by the agency involves the collection of personal information, the agency must also consider its obligations under the Privacy Act 1988 and the Australian Government Agencies Privacy Code.[41]

[^40]: For further information about the access to information icon see Icons for access to information.
[^41]: See About the Australian Government Agencies Privacy Code | OAIC.

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Publication on a website
title: Publication on a website
text:
Guidance on publishing information is available at the following places:
- the Digital Service Standard, which encourages agencies to consider appropriate tools and systems already used by government (Criterion 4), contains advice on using open standards and common platforms (Criterion 7), and advice about making online material accessible (Criterion 9)[42]
- the Australian Human Rights Commission, Guidelines on equal access to digital goods and services, discussed below at [13.168]
- guidance on implementing metadata for the web is available on the National Australian Archives (NAA) site[43]
- the Australian Government Style Manual provides advice on meta tags, keywords and structure to make content discoverable through the major search engines.

[^42]: See Digital Service Standard | digital.gov.au. For the full Digital Experience Policy, which encompasses 4 standards that form the core requirements for delivering consistent and high-quality digital government services see Digital Experience | digital.gov.au.
[^43]: See Metadata for the web | naa.gov.au.

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Publication on a website
title: Publication on a website
text: Some smaller agencies may not maintain their own website but have a homepage on the website of another agency, usually the portfolio department. The same principles apply to the IPS entries of these smaller agencies as they do to the host agency’s website.

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Publication on a website
title: Publication on a website
text: Agencies can also publish information that is part of their IPS entry on another website (s 8D(3)(b)). One website is www.data.gov.au which has been established to facilitate the publication of datasets for use by the commercial, research and community sectors. Other websites that publish information from across government are www.legislation.gov.au (a compilation of Australian Government legislation) and www.directory.gov.au (the Government Online Directory).

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Structure of agency IPS entry
title: Structure of agency IPS entry
text: The FOI Act specifies the information an agency must publish under the IPS, but not the format of publication. The FOI Act does not require that agencies use the headings or language specified in s 8(2). However it will be easier for the public to find information published by each agency under the IPS if there is a consistent presentation of information across agency websites.

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Structure of agency IPS entry
title: Structure of agency IPS entry
text:
Agencies may consider, where practicable, using the following headings in their publication framework. The information provided under those headings may extend beyond the categories of information described in s 8(2).
- Agency plan
  - The agency plan as required by s 8(2)(a)
- Who we are
  - The organisation and structure of the agency, the location of offices, governance arrangements, senior management team and statutory appointments referred to in s 8(2)(d)
- What we do
  - A description of the functions and powers of the agency, and the rules, guidelines, practices and precedents relating to those functions and powers (that is, operational information); including a link to operational information if published on another webpage
- Our reports and responses to Parliament
  - Annual reports laid before the Parliament, and other information routinely provided to the Parliament
- Routinely requested information and disclosure log
  - Information to which the agency routinely gives access in response to FOI requests and the disclosure log of information that has been released under the FOI Act
- Consultation arrangements
  - Consultation arrangements that enable members of the public to comment on specific policy proposals for which the agency is responsible
- Our priorities
  - For example, the corporate and strategic plans of the agency, and assessments and reviews undertaken of agency programs
- Our finances
  - For example, financial information relating to pay and grading structures in the agency, procurement procedures, tendering and contracts
- Our lists
  - For example, agency contracts, grants and appointments, links to datasets published by the agency, information held in registers required by law, and other lists and registers relating to the agency’s functions
- Contact us
  - The contact details of an officer (or officers) who can be contacted about access to the agency’s information under the FOI Act.

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Accuracy and currency of published information
title: Accuracy and currency of published information
text: Each agency’s IPS entry is required to be ‘accurate, up-to-date and complete’ (s 8B).

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Accuracy and currency of published information
title: Accuracy and currency of published information
text:
The action an agency should take to comply with that requirement may vary according to the nature of the information in the IPS entry. The following is given as a general guide for agencies, but does not diminish the obligation of agencies to ensure compliance with s 8B:
- Some categories of information should be updated as soon as reasonably practicable after any change to that information — for example, information about the structure of the agency, senior officers, statutory appointments, contact arrangements and reports that have been laid before the Parliament.
- Operational information should be updated in the IPS at the same time a revised or updated version of the information is provided to agency officers.
- Other categories of information can be updated on a periodic basis, following a scheduled agency review of the accuracy, currency and completeness of the information. For example, the agency plan and information that is routinely provided to the Parliament or in response to FOI requests. It is advisable to include a notation on the document that is published under the IPS indicating when it was last published or updated. It is also advisable when creating a document that is published to consider when it would be appropriate to review the content.
- Consultation arrangements should be updated as soon as a new or varied arrangement is established.
- Any change to an agency’s functions or powers, especially a change resulting from a legislative amendment or alteration of an executive scheme, should be updated as soon as reasonably practicable.
- Agencies should bear in mind that other FOI Act provisions are relevant to the agency’s publishing obligations. Specifically, information must be published on a disclosure log within 10 days of release under the FOI Act (s 11C(6)), and a person cannot be subjected to any prejudice as a result of not having access to unpublished operational information (s 10).
- If an agency has multiple versions of a document that contain minor and insignificant variations (for example, training materials), it will be sufficient compliance with s 8(2) for the agency to publish one representative and current version of the document.
- Information published on a website can later be removed from the website and archived, as long as details are published of how the information can be obtained if the agency is still required to publish that information under s 8(2).

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Accessibility
title: Accessibility
text: Information that forms part of the IPS must be published ‘to members of the public generally’ (s 8D(2)(a)) and, if an agency considers it appropriate to do so, ‘to particular classes of persons or entities’ (s 8D(2)(b)).

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Accessibility
title: Accessibility
text:
Accessibility of published information by all members of the community is an important principle underlying the IPS. Three requirements reinforce this principle:
- Section 24 of the Disability Discrimination Act 1992 provides that it is unlawful for a person (including a government agency) to provide goods or services to a person with a disability less favourably than to a person without that disability.
- Government agencies are required to conform to the latest applicable WCAG standard.[44] New web content needs to conform to these standards as far as possible.
- The Australian Human Rights Commission has published Guidelines on equal access to digital goods and services which endorses compliance with WCAG 2.2 Level AA. The Human Rights Commission suggests that agencies also consider appropriate Level AAA success criteria such as video transcripts, audio contrast, clear links and section headings.[45]

[^44]: See Australian Government Style Manual. Also see Criterion 4. Make it accessible | digital.gov.au, from the Digital Transformation Agency’s Digital Inclusion Standard (‘Make It Accessible’). Criterion 4 says that Australian Government agencies need to make their digital services accessible and comply with all relevant legislation and standards, including the Disability Discrimination Act 1992, the latest version of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) and the Australian Government Style Manual. The Australian Government currently requires agencies to comply with WCAG 2.2 AA standards (see the Australian Government Style Guide). Further information about WCAG compliance see Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2.
[^45]: See Australian Human Rights Commission Guidelines on equal access to digital goods and services , (April 2025), p 43. The Australian Human Rights Commission endorses the use of WCAG 2.2 AA, but asks agencies to consider appropriate Level AAA success criteria such as video transcripts, audio contrast, clear links and section headings (see Guidelines on equal access to digital goods and services).

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Charges
title: Charges
text: Subject to a limited exception, information published under the IPS must be available free of charge. An agency may charge for information under the IPS only where the information cannot be downloaded from a website and the agency has incurred specific reproduction or incidental costs in giving a person access to that information under the IPS (s 8D(4)). The details of the charge must be published under the IPS before any charge is imposed (s 8D(5)).

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Charges
title: Charges
text:
For example, information may be contained in a recording that cannot be readily converted to electronic format for publication and download from a website.[46] The agency can instead publish details of how the information may be obtained, including the charge that may be imposed for making it available in a suitable format (s 8D(3)(c)).

[^46]: Explanatory Memorandum to the Freedom of Information Amendment (Reform) Bill 2010, p 8.

heading: Managing an agency IPS entry > Charges
title: Charges
text:
A charge for IPS access is separate to the charges that can be imposed for processing FOI requests under the Charges Regulations.[47] The Charges Regulations may, however, provide useful guidance to an agency in calculating or imposing a charge for access under the IPS. The Charges Regulations are discussed in Part 4 of these Guidelines.

[^47]: Explanatory Memorandum to the Freedom of Information Amendment (Reform) Bill 2010, p 8.

heading: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers
title: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers
text:
The FOI Act confers 3 specific functions on the Information Commissioner for reviewing the operation of the IPS (s 8F):
- reviewing the operation of the IPS in each agency, in conjunction with the agency
- investigating an agency’s compliance with IPS requirements, either upon receipt of a complaint or at the Information Commissioner’s initiative
- otherwise monitoring, investigating and reporting on the operation of the IPS.

heading: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers
title: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers
text: Each of those functions is described in more detail below.

heading: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers > Review of agency IPS compliance
title: Review of agency IPS compliance
text: Each agency must complete a review of its IPS compliance at least once every 5 years (s 9(1)). The review must be undertaken in conjunction with the Information Commissioner. The OAIC encourages agencies to undertake more regular reviews, preferably annually.

heading: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers > Review of agency IPS compliance
title: Review of agency IPS compliance
text:
The OAIC conducted major surveys of IPS compliance in 2012, 2018 and 2023 and plans to undertake a further review in 2028.[48] Agencies can use the survey results to help improve their IPS performance.

[^48]: The survey reports are available at Information Publication Scheme review survey 2012 | OAIC; Information Publication Scheme review survey 2018 | OAIC and Information Publication Scheme review survey 2023 | OAIC.

heading: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers > Review of agency IPS compliance
title: Review of agency IPS compliance
text:
In undertaking a review, agencies should focus on the following 5 key elements of IPS compliance when undertaking the s 9 review:
1. Agency plan — has the agency published a comprehensive plan for its IPS compliance?
2. Governance and administration — does the agency have appropriate governance mechanisms in place to meet its IPS obligations, including an information management framework?
3. IPS document holdings — has the agency reviewed its document holdings to decide what information must be published under s 8(2) and further information that can be published under s 8(4)? Is the agency IPS entry accurate, up-to-date and complete?
4. Structure of the IPS — does the agency have a publication framework in place and has it taken the necessary steps to ensure that information in its IPS entry is easily discoverable and accessible to the Australian community?
5. Agency compliance review — does the agency have appropriate processes, systems and resources in place to monitor and review its IPS compliance and to make necessary improvement in the agency’s IPS implementation?

heading: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers > Investigations and complaints
title: Investigations and complaints
text:
The Information Commissioner can investigate complaints about an agency’s IPS compliance (s 70). The Information Commissioner publishes summaries of investigation outcomes, including the outcomes of investigations into complaints about agency compliance with the IPS requirements. [49]

[^49]: See 20211122-Outcomes-of-investigations-summary-table.pdf.

heading: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers > Investigations and complaints
title: Investigations and complaints
text: The Information Commissioner can also undertake a Commissioner initiated investigation into an agency’s performance of functions or exercise of powers under the FOI Act (s 69(2)). For more information see Part 11 of these Guidelines.

heading: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers > Investigations and complaints
title: Investigations and complaints
text: An agency’s IPS obligations are not subject to IC review under Part VII of the FOI Act.

heading: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers > Monitoring and reporting
title: Monitoring and reporting
text: The Information Commissioner is required to prepare an annual report on the OAIC’s operations (Australian Information Commissioner Act 2010 s 30). The Information Commissioner will include in the annual report information on the administration of the IPS by agencies.

heading: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers > Monitoring and reporting
title: Monitoring and reporting
text:
Section 93 of the FOI Act requires agencies to provide the Information Commissioner with information required to prepare an annual report.[50]

[^50]: See FOI Statistics Guide.

heading: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers > Monitoring and reporting
title: Monitoring and reporting
text: For more information about reporting requirements see Part 15 of these Guidelines. Copyright

heading: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers > Monitoring and reporting
title: Monitoring and reporting
text: As noted in the guiding principles to these Guidelines (see [13.15] dot point 5), the Information Commissioner encourages agencies to make information they publish under the IPS available for reuse on open licensing terms, as far as that is reasonable and practicable to do. Agencies should have a clear statement on their websites, on their homepage, or on their IPS entry page about the extent to which the public can reuse material in which they hold copyright.

heading: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers > Monitoring and reporting
title: Monitoring and reporting
text:
In deciding on the appropriate licensing, agencies should consider the Australian Government Intellectual Property Manual[51] and the Guidelines on licensing public sector information for Australian Government entities.[52]

[^51]: Available at Australian Government intellectual property manual | Attorney-General's Department.
[^52]: Available at Guidelines on licensing public sector information for Australian Government entities | Attorney-General's Department .

heading: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers > Monitoring and reporting
title: Monitoring and reporting
text: While most of the information an agency publishes in its IPS entry will have been created by government, there may be documents in the agency’s possession where a third party (such as the author or publisher of the material) owns the copyright.

heading: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers > Monitoring and reporting
title: Monitoring and reporting
text: No action lies against the Commonwealth, a minister, an agency or an officer of any agency for breach of copyright, among other things, if the minister or an agency officer publishes a document in good faith, in the belief that publication is required or permitted under the IPS or the disclosure log provisions (s 90(1)(a)). However, this provision does not constitute authorisation or approval for reuse of the material, including by members of the public.

heading: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers > Monitoring and reporting
title: Monitoring and reporting
text:
Where a third party owns copyright in material an agency publishes as part of its IPS entry, the agency should include a clear statement on its website advising the public that they may need to seek permission from the copyright owner to reuse the material. A statement such as the following could be used:
To the extent that copyright in some of this material is owned by a third party, you may need to seek their permission before you can reuse that material.

heading: Information Commissioner’s IPS functions and powers > Monitoring and reporting
title: Monitoring and reporting
text: If an agency knows the details of third-party ownership of copyright in material it has published under the IPS, the agency should, with the copyright owner’s consent, provide contact details on its website, to help members of the public.

heading: Legal protection for discretionary/good faith publication
title: Legal protection for discretionary/good faith publication
text: The FOI Act provides legal protection where information has been published in good faith in the belief that publication was either required or permitted under the IPS (ss 90 and 92). The protection applies to the Commonwealth, a minister, an agency or an officer of an agency. The scope of the protection is that no action lies for defamation, breach of confidence or infringement of copyright or (as to ministers and agency officers) criminal liability.

heading: Legal protection for discretionary/good faith publication
title: Legal protection for discretionary/good faith publication
text: These protections complement the policy objective of the FOI Act to provide a secure framework for publication of Australian Government information. These protections are conditional and apply only where a minister or agency officer publishes a document in good faith in the belief that publication was required or permitted under the FOI Act.

heading: Legal protection for discretionary/good faith publication
title: Legal protection for discretionary/good faith publication
text: The legal protection provided by ss 90 and 92 also applies to the release of information in response to an FOI request, and to publication apart from the FOI Act where a minister or agency officer believes in good faith that publication is required or permitted. For more information about these protections see Part 3 of these Guidelines.

heading: Introduction
title: Introduction
text: Agencies and ministers must publish information that has been released in response to every FOI request, subject to certain exceptions (s 11C). This publication is known as a ‘disclosure log’.

heading: Introduction
title: Introduction
text: The requirement to publish a disclosure log complements the Information Publication Scheme (IPS) (see Part 13 of these Guidelines). Together these require agencies and, for the disclosure log, ministers, to publish a range of government information.

heading: Introduction
title: Introduction
text: The disclosure log facilitates publication of information released to individuals in response to FOI requests, to the general public. This reinforces the objects of the FOI Act that promote proactive publication of information (s 3(1)(a)) and in recognition that information held by government is a national resource (s 3(3)).

heading: Introduction
title: Introduction
text:
In publishing information released in response to FOI requests, agencies and ministers should take account of the ‘lowest reasonable cost’ object in s 3(4):
